warmup.q: Three nodes elect a leader. Each node votes once, a winner needs 2 of the 3 votes, and there is a proof that at most one node wins, even if a node crashes. In production two nodes win the same term after a node restarts. What went wrong?
options: The proof's arithmetic is wrong: 2 of 3 isn't a safe majority
The network delivered one vote twice
The proof assumed a crashed node never comes back, and the restarted node had forgotten its vote and voted again
Clock skew made the two winners see different terms
warmup.why: The arithmetic holds: there are 3 votes, and two winners would need 4. A duplicated message delivers the same vote again, which a candidate counts once. This protocol uses no clocks. The proof was right for its model, crash-stop, where a crashed node stays down. A node that keeps its vote in memory and restarts is outside that model: it comes back with empty memory and votes a second time. Which model a proof assumes is this lesson's subject.

sections.h: A proof holds only inside its model
sections.html:
Here is a small election. Three nodes, n1, n2 and n3, must pick one leader for term 1. n1 and n3 are candidates: each votes for itself and asks the other two for their votes. A node votes for the first candidate that asks and refuses everyone after that. A candidate with 2 of the 3 votes has won.

Is it safe? The argument fits in two lines. Each node votes once, so there are 3 votes in total. Two winners would need 4. So at most one node wins term 1, in any order of messages, and even if a node crashes, because a crashed node casts no more votes.

The argument is correct, and it assumes something it never says: that a crashed node stays crashed. Now let n1 keep its vote in memory, win, crash and restart. The process comes back with empty memory, believes it hasn't voted, and gives its vote to n3. n3 has 2 votes too. Two leaders in one term, and no line of the argument was wrong. The stepper below walks through it, and the lab's explorer finds it in a few milliseconds.

That's why every distributed algorithm is proved against a system model: a written list of the faults it must survive. For nodes, three models cover most of the literature:

  • crash-stop: a node works correctly until it stops, and it never comes back;
  • crash-recovery: a node can stop at any moment and start again later. Whatever it wrote to stable storage (a disk, after fsync) survives, and everything in memory is gone;
  • Byzantine: a node can do anything at all, including send false or contradictory messages (section 4).

The gray failures from lesson 2 of this track, a node that half works, sit between these and are the hardest to model.

Real servers restart, so crash-recovery is the realistic node model, and it tells you the fix: a node writes its vote to disk before it tells anyone. Raft does exactly this. Its paper lists votedFor as persistent state, updated on stable storage before the node responds (the Consistency and consensus track builds Raft). Writing the vote after replying is no better than never writing it, because a crash in between forgets a vote that someone has already counted.

That gap shows up in real systems. Jepsen's analysis of NATS 2.12.1 (December 2025) found that JetStream acknowledged messages at once but called fsync only every two minutes by default. A simulated power failure lost 131,418 of 930,005 acknowledged messages. The replication protocol assumed disks that kept what they'd been given, and the default configuration didn't provide them.

try.title: Explore every run of the election
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It checks the election from this section in every order of messages and at every possible moment for one crash, under each node model.

Before you read the table, predict the last column for each row: no crashes; crash-stop with the vote in memory; crash-recovery with the vote in memory, written to disk after the reply, and written before it.
Read the shortest failing trace it prints. Which node forgot what, and at which step would writing the vote to disk have saved it?
Optional: run it with -Pargs='5 1' for five nodes. The trace gets longer (10 steps) but the story is the same.
try.expect:
3 nodes, candidates n1 and n3, at most 1 crash(es). Rule: at most one node ever wins the term.

model           vote stored           states   stuck  one leader?
no crashes      memory only               36       0  yes
crash-stop      memory only              144       5  yes
crash-recovery  memory only                -       -  NO: broken after 6 steps
crash-recovery  disk, after reply          -       -  NO: broken after 6 steps
crash-recovery  disk, before reply        268       2  yes

The shortest way to break it (crash-recovery, memory only):
   1. n1 asks n2 for its vote
   2. n2's vote reaches n1
   3. n1 crashes
   4. n1 restarts
   5. n3 asks n1 for its vote
   6. n1's vote reaches n3
  winners of the term: n1 and n3

Without crashes and under crash-stop, all 36 and 144 reachable states have at most one winner. Under crash-recovery with the vote in memory, the explorer finds two winners after 6 steps. The node that forgot is the winner itself: n1 loses its own vote at the crash and gives it to n3 after the restart. Writing the vote to disk after replying fails the same way, because a crash can land between the reply and the write. Writing it before replying is safe in all 268 states. The stuck column is the next section's subject.

sections.h: Safety says nothing bad happens, liveness says something good eventually does
sections.html:
The explorer checked "at most one leader" in all 144 states of the crash-stop election and never saw it broken. But 5 of those states are dead ends: nothing more can happen, and nobody has won. In one, n2 crashed before it voted. n1 and n3 each hold their own vote, each refused the other, and both wait for n2 forever.

Those are two different kinds of promise, and every correctness property is one of them or a mix of both.

A safety property says that nothing bad ever happens: at most one leader per term; no card is charged twice for one idempotency key; a ledger balance never goes below zero. When one breaks, you can point at the moment it broke (the second leader won at step 6), and nothing done afterwards undoes it.

A liveness property says that something good eventually happens: every authorization eventually gets an approve or a decline; a leader is eventually elected; every replica eventually holds the same data. At any moment a liveness property may not hold yet and still hold later. The word "eventually" gives it away. So eventual consistency is a liveness property: on its own, it promises nothing about what a read returns right now.

The split tells you how to design. Safety must hold in every execution the system model allows: every order of messages, every crash, every pause, even with every node down at once. Liveness may depend on conditions you can name, such as "once a majority is up and messages arrive within a second for long enough, a leader is elected". A cluster that stalls during a network partition and carries on afterwards has kept its promises. A cluster that elects two leaders during the partition has not, and healing the partition doesn't fix it.

The dead ends also show what the election lacks: a way to give up and try again. Even the fixed election has 2 dead ends among its 268 states. In both, a candidate crashed and restarted with an empty tally, because a tally lives in memory, so the vote it counted after restarting was its only one. Real protocols add a timeout that starts a new term with fresh votes. That restores liveness and, as long as each node still votes at most once per term, costs no safety. Timeouts are where the next section begins.

try.title: Sort payment promises into safety and liveness
steps: For each promise, decide whether it is safety or liveness, and name the bad thing it rules out or the good thing it waits for.

1: an idempotency key is never used for two different payments. 2: every refund is eventually reflected in the merchant's balance. 3: the consumer never commits a Kafka offset past a record it hasn't processed. 4: the nightly settlement batch finishes by 06:00. 5: a paused lease holder's late write is refused.
For the liveness ones, write down what the system needs (which nodes up, what timing) for the promise to come true.
try.expect: 1, 3 and 5 are safety: each names a bad event (a reused key, a skipped record, a stale write accepted) that happens at one moment and can't be undone. 2 is liveness: at any moment the refund may not show yet, and it can still show later; it needs the consumer that applies refunds to be running and the log to be reachable. 4 is the surprise: a deadline turns progress into safety. At 06:00 you can point at the moment it broke, and finishing at 06:05 doesn't repair it. That's why "respond within 2 seconds" can be tested and enforced the way "respond eventually" can't.

sections.h: Timing models, FLP, and how timeouts get around it
sections.html:
The node model says what a node may do. The timing model says what you may assume about time: how long a message can take, how long a process can pause, how far a clock can drift. There are three.

A synchronous system has known upper bounds on all three. If no reply has come within the bound, the other node has crashed, and you know it. Lessons 1 to 4 of this track took that world apart: networks hold packets in queues for any length of time, garbage collection and VM migration stop processes for seconds, and clocks jump. Nobody can promise the bounds, so an algorithm proved in this model is proved for a system you don't have.

An asynchronous system has no bounds at all, and no clocks. A node can't even time out, because "too long" means nothing. An algorithm correct here is correct anywhere, but the model is so weak that some problems can't be solved in it.

The best-known example is the FLP result, named for Fischer, Lynch and Paterson (1985). In the asynchronous model, if even one node may crash, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee that the nodes reach consensus (agree on one value) and finish. In plain words: a node that hasn't answered may be dead or merely slow, and nothing tells the two apart. In every run some message is the one that would tip the decision. FLP shows that whoever controls the timing can keep delaying exactly that message, and because a delay looks like a crash, the algorithm can't wait for it forever and can't safely decide without it.

FLP doesn't say consensus is impossible in practice. It says termination can't be guaranteed in a model with no time in it, and real systems step outside that model. The partially synchronous model (Dwork, Lynch and Stockmeyer, 1988) says bounds exist and usually hold, but may be broken for a while, for a period nobody knows in advance. Algorithms for it, Paxos and Raft among them, are safe in every execution, including while the bounds are broken, and make progress once timing behaves. Raft uses timeouts for that: a follower that hears nothing for a random timeout (150 to 300 ms in the Raft paper's example) starts an election. A wrong timeout costs an extra election, never two leaders. Randomized algorithms are the other way out: they finish with probability 1.

Partial synchrony with crash-recovery is the realistic default, and the figure places the systems you use in it. When timing misbehaves, you see the liveness side. In November 2020 a switch at Cloudflare failed partially for about six minutes. The three-node etcd cluster couldn't keep a leader and went read-only, and the knock-on effects degraded Cloudflare's API and dashboard for 6 hours 33 minutes. Cloudflare's post called it a Byzantine failure. It was an omission fault (messages lost on some paths), and etcd stalled rather than disagreeing with itself.

sections.h: Byzantine faults: why one liar needs four nodes
sections.html:
A Byzantine node doesn't just stop. It lies: it sends different answers to different nodes, relays a message it never received, or votes twice. The name comes from Lamport, Shostak and Pease's 1982 paper, which framed the problem as generals agreeing on a plan of attack while some of them are traitors.

Try it with three nodes deciding one payment. The leader, node 0, has a verdict (approve or decline) and sends it to both followers. Each follower then tells the other what the leader said and decides by majority over what it heard. One node lies. The figure shows two worlds. In A the leader is honest and says APPROVE, and follower 2 tells follower 1 that the leader said DECLINE. In B the leader lies: it tells follower 1 APPROVE and follower 2 DECLINE, and follower 2 honestly passes that on. Follower 1 hears exactly the same thing in both worlds: APPROVE from the leader, DECLINE from follower 2. In A it must decide APPROVE, because an honest leader's verdict has to win. In B it must decide the same as follower 2, whose view is the mirror image of its own. No rule gets both right, and the lab checks every rule and every lie to confirm it.

With four nodes, each follower hears three verdicts: one from the leader and two relayed. One liar spoils at most one of the three, so the honest majority wins. If the liar is the leader, every honest follower hears the same three verdicts and reaches the same decision.

The general rule is that tolerating f Byzantine nodes takes at least 3f + 1. You can only wait for n − f replies, because f nodes may never answer. Up to f of the replies you got may be lies, so at least n − 2f are honest, and the honest ones must outnumber the liars: n − 2f > f, so n > 3f. For crashes only, 2f + 1 is enough, because a crashed node never says anything false.

PBFT (Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance, Castro and Liskov, OSDI 1999) made this usable: 3f + 1 replicas, a primary that orders requests, and three rounds of messages (pre-prepare, prepare, commit) with quorums of 2f + 1. It is safe without any timing assumption and makes progress under partial synchrony. Their replicated NFS ran only 3% slower than plain NFS. Protocols of the same family run public blockchains, where the nodes belong to parties who don't trust each other (CometBFT, the consensus engine of Cosmos chains, does BFT state machine replication). Aircraft and spacecraft computers need the same guarantees, because radiation flips bits in memory.

Your database almost certainly doesn't. It would cost a fourth replica and more message rounds for each fault you tolerate. It wouldn't stop bugs, because every replica runs the same code, and a bug that makes one replica lie makes them all lie the same way, unless you write four independent implementations. It wouldn't stop attackers either: an exploit that opens one replica usually opens all of them. Inside one organization, authentication, access control, encryption and firewalls do that job.

try.title: Let one node lie in every possible way
steps: Run the demo below. For 3, 4 and 5 nodes and each tie rule, it runs every round with one liar: each verdict the leader could hold, each node as the liar, every combination of lies.
Predict first: with 3 nodes, is there a tie rule that never fails? With 4?
Look at the last row. With 5 nodes a liar can't break the fixed tie rules, but it breaks the rule "on a tie, trust what the leader told you". Work out why from the decisions it prints.
try.expect:
nodes  on a tie  rounds  first round that breaks a rule
    3  approve       16  follower 1 lies (honest verdict DECLINE): validity, honest followers decide {2=APPROVE}
    3  decline       16  follower 1 lies (honest verdict APPROVE): validity, honest followers decide {2=DECLINE}
    3  leader        16  the leader lies (honest verdict APPROVE): agreement, honest followers decide {1=APPROVE, 2=DECLINE}
    4  approve       40  none
    4  decline       40  none
    4  leader        40  none
    5  approve       96  none
    5  decline       96  none
    5  leader        96  the leader lies (honest verdict APPROVE): agreement, honest followers decide {1=APPROVE, 2=APPROVE, 3=DECLINE, 4=DECLINE}

With 3 nodes every tie rule fails: a fixed rule lets a lying follower overrule an honest leader (validity), and trusting the leader lets a lying leader split the followers (agreement). With 4 nodes all 40 rounds pass under every rule, because each honest follower hears an odd number of verdicts and the liar spoils only one. With 5 nodes a lying leader can send 2 APPROVE and 2 DECLINE. Every honest follower then hears the same tie, and a fixed rule turns it into the same decision everywhere, but "trust the leader" makes each follower decide by its own message, so they split 2 and 2.

sections.h: Small lies: corrupted bits and wrong answers
sections.html:
Full Byzantine tolerance is rare, but small lies are common, and they need no attacker. Disks return data that differs from what was written: TigerBeetle's fault model plans for silent corruption on about 0.031% of SSDs and 1.4% of enterprise hard disks per year. CPUs compute wrong answers without crashing: Google's "Cores that don't count" (HotOS 2021) found a few such "mercurial" cores per several thousand machines. The What data systems are for track's lesson on faults met these as silent data corruption. In a replicated system they can be worse than a crash, because the system keeps going. In the same NATS analysis, corrupting data files on just one or two of five nodes lost 679,153 of 1,367,069 acknowledged writes in one run.

The defences are cheap. Put a checksum on every record or block you write, check it on every read, and carry it end to end, from the code that creates the data to the code that finally uses it. TCP and UDP carry a 16-bit checksum, but it is a plain sum, so it can't see two 16-bit words that swap places, and it only covers one hop between two kernels. Corruption in your process's memory or on a disk happens outside it. Use a stronger code such as CRC-32C (Kafka's record batches carry one, and the JDK has java.util.zip.CRC32C), or a cryptographic hash if someone might tamper with the data. Validate what you read: refuse an amount over the merchant's limit, a currency you don't know, a status outside the enum. And don't trust a single source for time: an NTP client asks several servers and drops the one that disagrees with the rest (lesson 3 of this track covers NTP).

A checksum proves only that the bytes didn't change after it was computed. A core that computes the wrong amount before the checksum is taken produces a perfect checksum of the wrong data. The Try it shows all three cases.

try.title: Three ways to damage a payment record
steps: Run the demo below. It damages one payment record three ways and checks each copy with the Internet checksum (the 16-bit sum TCP uses), with CRC-32C, and with a validation rule.
Predict which checks catch a single flipped bit, two 16-bit words swapped, and an amount that was wrong before anyone computed a checksum.
Read internetChecksum in the demo. Why can't any sum notice that two words changed places?
try.expect:
stored:   pay-7731|m-cafe|EUR|00004000|CAPTURED   inet=3694  crc32c=7d47b10e

one bit flipped:    pay-7731|m-cafe|EUR|00005000|CAPTURED   inet=3594  crc32c=4d95896b
                    inet caught, crc32c caught, validation: ok

two words swapped:  pay-7731|m-cafe|EUR|00400000|CAPTURED   inet=3694  crc32c=25d8d26f
                    inet MISSED, crc32c caught, validation: ok

wrong at source:    pay-7731|m-cafe|EUR|04000000|CAPTURED
                    inet passes, crc32c passes, validation: amount 40000.00 is over m-cafe's limit

One flipped bit turns 40.00 into 50.00, and both checksums catch it. Swapping two words turns it into 4,000.00: the Internet checksum is identical (3694), because addition doesn't care about order, while CRC-32C changes. Neither validation rule fires for 4,000.00, which is under the limit. The amount computed wrong at the source passes both checksums, since they were computed over the wrong bytes; only the business rule catches it, and only because the error was large.

refs.title: TigerBeetle: Safety (fault model and the VOPR)
Hochschild et al., Cores that don't count (HotOS 2021)

analogy: A system model is like the load rating on a bridge. The engineers prove the bridge carries 40 tonnes, assuming the steel matches its specification. Drive 60 tonnes over it, or build it from steel that is secretly weaker, and the proof says nothing, although every line of it is still right. An algorithm's proof works the same way: it holds for the faults on its list (crashes that stay crashed, disks that keep what was fsynced) and promises nothing outside them. The analogy breaks in how the failure shows. An overloaded bridge sags and creaks first. A protocol outside its model usually runs fine for months and then breaks safety in a single step, with no warning beforehand.
world: Your stack has already picked models for you. Kafka acknowledges an acks=all write once the in-sync replicas have it, and by default that means in their page cache, not fsynced to disk. Its model is that the replicas won't all lose power at once, which you make true by spreading brokers across racks or availability zones; three brokers on one power feed quietly leave the model. Oracle takes the stricter path: by default a COMMIT returns only after the log writer has written the redo to disk. For each store, ask which faults your deployment can produce that its model leaves out: a VM whose disk cache acknowledges flushes it hasn't made, a member restored from an old disk image. And notice where you already defend against liars. The card issuer is outside your trust boundary, so your code checks that an authorization response has the right shape and the amount you asked for. That validation is your Byzantine fault tolerance. Nobody runs PBFT with an issuer.
mistake: The common mistake is breaking the crash-recovery assumption under a consensus system without noticing: putting etcd, ZooKeeper or KRaft controllers on storage that acknowledges writes it hasn't made durable, turning off fsync because a benchmark ran faster, or restoring one member's disk from an old snapshot so it rejoins with last week's votes and log. Each gives a node amnesia, which is the restart from section 1, and the algorithm's proof no longer covers you. It happens because nothing breaks at once: the cluster runs fine until a crash lands in the gap. Keep fsync on for anything that votes or acknowledges. To rebuild a member, remove it from the cluster and add it back as a new, empty member, which the protocol knows how to bring up to date, instead of copying old state into it.

compare.title: Reply, then write, against write, then reply

a.label: Reply, then write (unsafe)
a.title: a crash between the two lines forgets a counted vote
a.html: fun onRequestVote(req: RequestVote) { if (votedFor != null) return reply(req.from, granted = false) votedFor = req.from // in memory only, for now reply(req.from, granted = true) // the candidate may count this vote... disk.writeAndSync("votedFor", req.from) // ...before this line runs }

b.label: Write, then reply (safe)
b.title: what Raft requires
b.html: fun onRequestVote(req: RequestVote) { if (votedFor != null) return reply(req.from, granted = false) votedFor = req.from disk.writeAndSync("votedFor", req.from) // survives a crash once this returns reply(req.from, granted = true) // only now may anyone count it } // on restart: votedFor = disk.read("votedFor")

compare.note: The two functions differ only in the order of two lines, and under crash-stop both are correct, because a node that crashes between them never comes back. Under crash-recovery the left one has a window, between the reply and the write, in which a crash makes the node forget a vote the candidate has already counted. The right one closes it: by the time anyone hears of the vote, a restart will find it. The price is one synchronous disk write per vote, which is why consensus systems care so much about fsync latency.

worked.title: Why one liar needs four nodes, step by step

steps.say: Fix the fault budget: at most f nodes are faulty. A faulty node may never answer, so a decision can't wait for more than n − f replies.
steps.code: val replies = n - f // the f you don't hear from may be crashed or silent on purpose

steps.say: Of the replies you did get, up to f may come from liars: the silent nodes could be honest ones that are merely slow. So at least n − 2f of your replies are honest.
steps.code: val honest = replies - f // n - 2f, in the worst case

steps.say: The honest replies must outvote the lies. Solve for n.
Do the same for crash faults. A crashed node says nothing false, so every reply is honest. What you need instead is that any two groups of n − f replies share a node, so two decisions can't both win.
Put numbers on it. With Byzantine faults a quorum is 2f + 1 of 3f + 1 nodes, and any two quorums overlap in at least f + 1 nodes, so at least one honest node sits in both.
steps.code: fun nodesFor(f: Int, byzantine: Boolean) = if (byzantine) 3 * f + 1 else 2 * f + 1 // f = 1: 3 nodes for crashes, 4 for liars // f = 2: 5 nodes for crashes, 7 for liars // overlap of two quorums: 2 * (2f + 1) - (3f + 1) = f + 1

lab.title: Model-check an election, then out-vote a liar
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 20 fail: 6 in ExplorerTest, 9 in ElectionTest and 5 in GeneralsTest.

In Explorer.kt, write explore: a breadth-first search over states, with a parent map that also serves as the visited set. Run --tests 'sfz.dist.l07.ExplorerTest' until its 6 tests pass. Its first model is the lost update from the Transactions track, found this time by a machine.

In Election.kt, write recover. Run ElectionTest: the crash-stop tests pass, and under crash-recovery with votes in memory the explorer finds two leaders in 6 steps. Three tests still fail, because the stub's castVote keeps every vote in memory whatever persist says. Fix it.
In Generals.kt, write decide. GeneralsTest then runs every round with one liar for 3, 4 and 5 nodes.
Read the last test in GeneralsTest. Explain to yourself why, with 5 nodes, breaking ties toward the leader's own message fails when a fixed tie rule doesn't.
hints: Check the invariant when you take a state off the front of the queue. Breadth-first order then makes the first broken state one of the closest, and traceTo(s, parent) gives you its trace.
if (t in parent) continue before parent[t] = s to label is all the loop protection you need: a state already seen is never queued again.
recover is one copy: up = true, memVote = node.diskVote, unflushed = false, votes = emptySet().
In castVote, BEFORE_REPLY sets both memVote and diskVote; AFTER_REPLY sets memVote and unflushed = true, and the given flush step does the rest.
In decide, count the approvals in relayed, plus one if fromLeader is APPROVE; the declines are the rest of the relayed.size + 1 votes.

drill.title: Write the explorer from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write explore(initial, next, invariant): a breadth-first search that returns the shortest list of step labels leading to a state that breaks the invariant, or null if none does. Then say in one line each why its trace is a shortest one and why it ends on a model whose states form a loop.

answer.html: fun <S> explore(initial: S, next: (S) -> List<Pair<String, S>>, invariant: (S) -> Boolean): List<String>? { val parent = HashMap<S, Pair<S, String>?>() // how each state was first reached; also "seen" val queue = ArrayDeque(listOf(initial)) parent[initial] = null while (queue.isNotEmpty()) { val s = queue.removeFirst() if (!invariant(s)) { // walk the parents back to the start val trace = ArrayDeque<String>() var at = s while (true) { val (from, step) = parent.getValue(at) ?: break trace.addFirst(step) at = from } return trace.toList() } for ((step, t) in next(s)) { if (t !in parent) { parent[t] = s to step queue.addLast(t) } } } return null } // Shortest: a FIFO queue hands out every state 1 step away before any state 2 steps away. // Ends on loops: a state already in `parent` is never queued again, and the model has finitely many states.

recap: An algorithm is proved against a system model: a timing model and a node model. Outside the model the proof says nothing, even when every line of it is right.
Crash-recovery is the realistic node model: memory is lost, disk survives. Anything another node may count, a vote or an acknowledgement, must be on disk before you send it.
Safety: nothing bad ever happens, and it must hold in every execution. Liveness: something good eventually happens, and it may wait for timing to behave. "Eventually" means liveness.

FLP: with no timing assumptions and one possible crash, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee that consensus finishes. Raft and Paxos assume partial synchrony: always safe, live once timeouts work.
Tolerating f lying nodes takes 3f + 1 (PBFT, quorums of 2f + 1); crashes need 2f + 1. Databases skip it because identical code lies identically and one exploit opens every node.
Small lies (flipped bits, wrong answers from a CPU) are common and cheap to catch: end-to-end checksums such as CRC-32C, validation of meaning, several clock sources.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our consensus library is formally proved, so we can't lose data." Explain what the proof covers and what it doesn't, using the election from this lesson.
explain.answer: The proof covers the system model it was written for, which for most consensus libraries is crash-recovery nodes with durable disks and partially synchronous timing. Inside that model it really is a guarantee: no order of messages and no crash breaks safety. Outside it, the proof says nothing. If a node acknowledges before it fsyncs, if the storage lies about flushes, or if we restore a member from an old disk image, that node can restart having forgotten a vote or a log entry it already gave out. That is the election from the lesson: n1 forgot its own vote, voted again, and two leaders won one term, with every line of the proof still correct. The proof also promises only safety without conditions; progress depends on timeouts working, so in a bad partition the cluster may stall. The useful question is whether our deployment stays inside the model: fsync on, replicas in separate failure domains, and members rebuilt as new members rather than restored from old copies.

deeper.html:
Every property splits in two. Alpern and Schneider (1985) proved that every property of a system's executions is the intersection of a safety property and a liveness property. "Every payment request gets the correct answer" is safety (never a wrong answer) plus liveness (eventually an answer). Writing the two halves down separately tells you which half your design must protect at all costs.

Timeouts as failure detectors. Chandra and Toueg (1996) recast timeouts as an unreliable failure detector: a module that suspects nodes and may be wrong. They showed consensus is solvable with one that keeps suspecting crashed nodes and eventually stops suspecting at least one correct node, however often it is wrong before that. It is the precise version of "timeouts are only suspicions" from lesson 2 of this track.

Randomness. Ben-Or (1983) gave a consensus protocol for the asynchronous model that escapes FLP with coin flips: it never decides wrongly, and the chance that it hasn't decided after k rounds shrinks towards zero. Raft's random election timeouts use randomness for the same purpose, to break ties that a deterministic schedule could repeat forever.

Signatures change the generals problem. Lamport, Shostak and Pease also showed that if every message is signed so that a liar can't forge what the leader said, the generals problem can be solved with any number of traitors. Practical BFT systems sign or authenticate messages, but replication under partial synchrony still needs 3f + 1 replicas.

The framing of this lesson (system models, safety and liveness, Byzantine faults and weak lying) follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 9. The lab's election and the payment examples are this course's own.
